Chapter Six: Building Indistractable Relationships—Communicating Boundaries and Modeling Focus
Let’s take things a step further. Up to now, we’ve talked a lot about building habits for our own focus, but what happens when distraction creeps into our relationships? The truth is, it’s not just a personal struggle—it spreads across families, friendships, and even our workplaces.
The way we connect with each other can make it easier—or so much harder—to stay focused. So, how do you actually build indistractable relationships? It starts with two things: communicating boundaries with care, and modeling the kind of focus you hope to see in others.
Here’s the first principle to keep in mind: attention is a shared resource. Have you ever tried talking to someone who keeps glancing at their phone or just seems half-there? It’s subtle, but over time, those moments chip away at trust and connection. It sends the message that the phone—or whatever’s on it—matters more than the person right in front of you.
So, what can you do about it? Start by setting clear expectations around your attention. Maybe you let your family know when you need some uninterrupted time, or you set up “device-free” zones during meals. The magic is in how you approach these conversations. Instead of making strict demands, try sharing the intention behind your boundaries. Show a little empathy.
For example, you might say, “Hey, I’d really love if we could all put our phones away at dinner. It helps me feel more connected to you, and I hope it helps you feel heard, too.” Or in a partnership, you can agree to carve out time each night just to talk—no distractions. It’s about being present, together.
Here are a few tips for communicating boundaries in your relationships:
- Share your reasons for needing focused time, and connect it to what you both value. - Invite others to share their needs, so you can find solutions that work for everyone. - Use gentle reminders and celebrate the little wins, rather than pointing out what’s going wrong.
Now, let’s talk about modeling focus. This is where your actions speak louder than words. When you consistently honor your own boundaries—let’s say, you don’t check messages during family time—people notice. And they’re more likely to follow your lead. You’re creating a kind of “culture of attention,” where everyone feels seen and supported.
Some ways to model focus for others? Be fully present in conversations. Put away your devices, make eye contact, and really listen. If you slip up—and hey, we all do—acknowledge it. No need for harsh self-judgment. Just recommit to what matters to you. And don’t forget to celebrate those small wins, like a device-free dinner or a focused work session.
By weaving these habits into your daily life, you turn your relationships into a true source of support for your focus—not a source of distraction.
So, here’s the key takeaway: indistractability isn’t just something you do on your own. It’s a shared journey, one that gets stronger when you bring others along with you.
